text:
THE eighth book of Suetonius' Lives of the Caesars contains his
account of the three Flavian emperors, and this first chapter is
a general introduction to the whole, giving (1) an estimate of the
dynasty, (2) an account of its ancestry. The life of Vespasian
proper begins with c. 2 Vespasianus natus est; cf. Titus...natus
est (Tit. 1), Domitianus natus est (Dom. 1).

Suetonius gives no account of Vespasian's activities between
the siege of Jotapata and his salutation as emperor (about two
years). In the course of two campaigns in 67 and 68 he occupied
and subdued the whole of Judaea except cept the city of Jerusalem
(Tac. Hist. 5. 10). As he was about to proceed to this final task,
he heard of the death of Nero, an event which automatically put an
end to his appointment (Jos. B. I. 4. 9. 2): he waited therefore for
further news. The news that came was of the accession of Galba,
and Titus was sent to pay homage to him, it was rumoured with the
hope that he would be adopted by the childless old emperor (Tac.
Hist. 2. 1): a contradictory rumour asserted that Galba had sent
assassins to murder Vespasian (Suet. Galb. 23). Anyway, when
Titus reached Corinth he heard of Galba's assassination, and
decided to return to Judaea, where both the Judaean and the Syrian
armies had already taken the oath of allegiance to Otho (Tac. Hist.
2. 1-6; Suet. Tit. 5). Finally, when the news of the first battle of
Bedriacum and of the death of Otho reached the East, they likewise
took the oath of allegiance to Vitellius, unwillingly, Vespasian being
not yet ready to declare himself (Tac. Hist. 2. 74).

This pressure of cases before the civil courts was one of the
natural results of the wars of 69: the prolonged cessation of justice
caused by them had resulted in the postponement and accumulation of normal cases, and the volume of these was swelled by the
abnormal disputes as to ownership of property inevitable after the
successive confiscations and grants of rival commanders. Vespasian's
commissioners were appointed (1) to adjudicate these ownership-ofproperty disputes, (2) to review the list of cases up before the
centumviri and to deal themselves with those which appeared
unnecessary or easy of settlement. Since the courts of the centumviri provided now the chief opportunity for ambitious advocates to
display their talents, their business was often unduly protracted by
forensic eloquence; Pliny shows himself an avowed supporter of
their lengthy and leisurely procedure (Ep. 1. 20; 6. 2).
